screens.title: Debugging with the Serial Port (UART)
screens.subtitle: Use UART0 to send text to a PC and inspect program behavior in embedded systems.

narration.text: Debugging embedded code often means you need to build your own display. The serial port, or UART, is the most common way to do that. On the TM4C123G LaunchPad the UART0 peripheral is routed to the USB debugger, so the same USB cable used for programming and power gives you a virtual COM port on your computer. That means you can print messages, numbers, and state to a terminal program and watch how your firmware behaves in real time. In this lesson you will learn how to enable clocks and set GPIO pins for UART0, compute integer and fractional baud divisors for a given system clock, configure line parameters like eight data bits and one stop bit, and implement simple send and string routines. You will also build a printf-style debugging flow by sending characters one at a time. By the end you should be able to open a terminal at 115200 baud, see messages from the board, and use prints to understand program state. Think of the serial port as a minimal but powerful window into your running device — a reliable way to prove what your code is doing and why an observed behavior occurs.

keyIdea.title: Why UART debugging matters
keyIdea.text: UART0 gives you a simple text channel from device to PC so you can print values, errors, and program flow without needing a display. It’s the foundational embedded debugging technique.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Debugging with the Serial Port
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Serial debugging with UART0

Open a virtual COM port to print program state, variable values, and error messages from your board. This is the primary way to observe behavior when no display is available.

16:9 HD Classroom
TM4C123G | UART0 → USB debug
What you will understand
  • How to enable UART0 and the GPIO pins it uses.
  • How baud divisors are computed from the system clock.
  • How to send characters and implement a simple printf-style printer.
Why it matters

Printing runtime values is the easiest and most portable way to confirm system state, troubleshoot faulty sensors, and verify control loops when hardware debuggers or displays are not practical.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you should be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure UART0 for PC communication, send and receive characters, use printf-style debugging, and understand the key serial parameters. First, configuring UART0 means enabling peripheral clocks and selecting alternate functions for the pins used by the module. This is important because a misconfigured clock or pin leaves the UART silent. Second, sending and receiving characters requires checking the flag register so you don’t write when the transmit FIFO is full and you properly read when data is available. Third, printf-style debugging is simply sending characters one at a time to represent formatted values, which lets you print counters, switch states, and error messages. Finally, knowing baud rate, data bits, stop bits, and parity ensures both ends speak the same framing language; a mismatch here is the most common cause of garbled output. Each objective maps to a small, practical milestone you can verify: see text in a terminal at 115200, confirm counts from 0 to 100, and compute divisors for alternate baud rates. These skills let you observe internal device state without a display or heavy debugger.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Checks
screens.subtitle: How to validate each objective with a simple experiment

narration.text: Learning objectives become real when you test them. For UART0 configuration, validate by enabling the peripheral and toggling a transmit; if the terminal shows text, the clock and alternate function are set correctly. For sending and receiving characters, practice writing a small routine that checks the transmit full flag before writing and then reads back characters to confirm reception. For printf-style debugging, implement a function that sends formatted digits and newline sequences and verify counters in the PC terminal. For serial framing and baud, always check that both the board and terminal use the same baud, data bits, and stop bits — 115200 with eight data bits and one stop bit is the standard for these examples. A short hands-on test is to make the board print a counted sequence from 0 to 100, open a terminal at 115200, and observe consistent numbers. If output is missing or garbled, use the checklist steps covered in this chapter to isolate whether the issue is a clock, pin configuration, divisor calculation, or terminal mismatch. Each validation step teaches you to connect a cause to an observable symptom.

keyIdea.title: Practice makes diagnostics reliable
keyIdea.text: A short verification script that prints known values lets you confirm correct configuration before adding complex logic.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Learning Objectives — Practice
Objective checklist
  1. Configure UART0: Enable SYSCTL clocks and confirm PA0/PA1 act as UART pins.
  2. Send/Receive: Implement a send-char routine that waits for the transmit FIFO to accept data.
  3. Printf-style: Print counters or switch states and verify in the terminal.
  4. Framing & baud: Use 115200, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity for examples in this chapter.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Quick experiment

Upload a small program that initializes UART0 and prints numbers from 0 to 100 at 115200. Open a terminal and confirm you see each number on its own line. This isolates configuration from your application logic.

Common failure modes
  • Wrong baud settings cause garbled or unreadable text.
  • Pins left in GPIO mode instead of their alternate function remain silent.
  • Forgetting to enable the peripheral clock prevents the UART from responding.

screens.title: What is a UART and why use it for debugging?
screens.subtitle: Definition, key properties, and a practical debugging scenario

narration.text: A UART, or Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter, is a hardware peripheral that sends and receives serial data without a shared clock. That means both sides agree on a baud rate — the number of bits per second — and then use start and stop bits to mark each byte. For debugging, UARTs are ideal because they convert program state and values into human-readable text you can view on a PC. Practically, you format messages with numbers and status strings, send them over UART0 on the LaunchPad, and read them in a terminal program. A concrete scenario: you have a sensor read routine that sometimes returns implausible values. Placing a serial print that shows the raw ADC value and a timestamp for each read lets you spot when the reading jumps and correlate that with other events. A common misconception is thinking UART needs a dedicated display; instead it uses the existing USB debugger as a virtual COM port on the computer. Another misconception is that UART is slow; while it can be slower than a parallel bus, a baud like 115200 is fast enough for most debugging prints. Takeaway: a UART is a low-cost, pervasive way to make embedded code speak so you can verify behavior and find bugs quickly.

keyIdea.title: UART in one line
keyIdea.text: A UART is an asynchronous serial link that turns internal state into serial text so you can inspect it on a PC.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › What is a UART?
Definition

Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter

A UART sends bytes as a sequence of bits with start and stop framing. Both devices must agree on the baud rate and data format.

Key properties
  • Asynchronous: no shared clock, relies on agreed baud.
  • Framing: start bit, data bits (commonly 8), optional parity, stop bits.
  • Simple hardware interface: TX and RX signals mapped to pins.
Practical debugging scenario

Print sensor values and a short label each time you read the sensor. Watching the stream in the terminal reveals timing and incorrect ranges faster than stepping through code with a debugger.

Concrete example: terminal output
Hello, Embedded World!\r\n\n sensor=512 time=0.123s\r\n sensor=514 time=0.223s\r\n sensor=1023 time=0.323s\r\n
Common misconception

Thinking UART requires a special display. In fact, the PC terminal serves as the display and the USB debugger often provides a virtual COM connection to UART0.

Key Takeaway

UART turns internal values into readable text, making it the most accessible debugging channel on many boards.

screens.title: Steps to initialize UART0 on the TM4C123G
screens.subtitle: Concrete initialization sequence and why each step matters

narration.text: Initializing UART0 on the TM4C123G is a small sequence of actions that, when done in order, gets the peripheral ready to transmit and receive. Step one is enabling the system clock for UART0 and GPIO Port A. Without the clock the registers do not respond. Step two is enabling the alternate function for PA0 and PA1 and enabling their digital function; this ensures these pins behave as UART TX and RX rather than general-purpose input and output. Step three is disabling the UART while configuring it so no activity interferes with setup. Step four sets the baud rate by writing integer and fractional divisors — these values determine how the UART samples the bitstream. Step five configures line control for eight data bits, one stop bit, no parity, and enables FIFOs for smoother data handling. The final step is enabling the UART transmitter and receiver in the control register. A common mistake is failing to wait for clocks to stabilize or leaving the pins in GPIO mode, which produces silence on the terminal. To verify success, implement a simple send-char routine and attempt to print a known string; seeing the string confirms a correct initialization sequence. How might you check each register to verify the configuration in your code?

keyIdea.title: Initialization checklist
keyIdea.text: Enable clocks, set pin alternate functions, program baud divisors, set line control, then enable the UART.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Initialize UART0
Process Flow

Initialization steps

  1. Enable clock: SYSCTL_RCGCUART_R |= 0x01; SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R |= 0x01; then wait for stability.
  2. Pin setup: GPIO_PORTA_AFSEL_R |= 0x03; GPIO_PORTA_DEN_R |= 0x03; make PA0/PA1 UART pins.
  3. Disable UART: clear UART0_CTL_R while changing settings.
  4. Baud rate: program UART0_IBRD_R and UART0_FBRD_R for the desired baud.
  5. Line control: set UART0_LCRH_R for 8N1 and enable FIFOs (0x70 in the example).
  6. Enable UART: set UART0_CTL_R |= 0x01 to allow TX and RX.
Why each step matters
  • Clock: register writes have no effect without a running peripheral clock.
  • Pin AF: pins default to GPIO and must be switched to the UART function to carry serial data.
  • Baud divisors: wrong numbers produce unreadable or garbled output at the PC.
Concrete example

With a 16 MHz system clock, setting IBRD=8 and FBRD=44 yields 115200 baud as shown in the provided code. Verify by printing a fixed string and watching the terminal.

Key Takeaway

Follow the enable-config-enable pattern and verify each step by printing a known string.

screens.title: UART0 initialization code example
screens.subtitle: Walk through the key lines from the supplied C initializer

narration.text: Let's walk through the UART0 initialization code line by line to understand what each register write does. First, the code sets the system control run-mode clock gating registers for UART and GPIO so the hardware receives a clock. Waiting for the GPIO clock to stabilize is important because subsequent writes to GPIO registers need the clock active. Next, the alternate function and digital enable registers for Port A set PA0 and PA1 to act as the UART pins and make them digital. The code then disables UART0 by clearing the control register bit; this prevents unintended transmissions while configuring. Baud is calculated for a 16 MHz system clock: BRD equals 16,000,000 divided by 16 times the baud; the integer and fractional parts are written to UART0_IBRD_R and UART0_FBRD_R respectively. UART0_LCRH_R is set to enable eight data bits and FIFOs by writing 0x70. Finally, UART0_CTL_R is set to enable the UART. A common misconception is that you can adjust baud without disabling the UART; changing divisors while active can cause transient errors. Verify success by calling the send-string routine to print a greeting. Which register would you read to confirm there is data ready to be read?

keyIdea.title: Code to behavior mapping
keyIdea.text: Each register write corresponds to a specific hardware behavior: clocks, pin function, baud generation, framing, and enabling.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Code Walkthrough
Example C
// Enable clock for UART0 and GPIO Port A\nSYSCTL_RCGCUART_R |= 0x01;\nSYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R |= 0x01;\n// Wait for clocks to stabilize\nwhile ((SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R & 0x01) == 0) {}\n\n// Set PA0/PA1 to UART\nGPIO_PORTA_AFSEL_R |= 0x03;\nGPIO_PORTA_DEN_R |= 0x03;\n\n// Disable UART while configuring\nUART0_CTL_R &= ~0x01;\n// Set baud: IBRD=8 FBRD=44 for 115200 with 16 MHz\nUART0_IBRD_R = 8;\nUART0_FBRD_R = 44;\n// 8 data bits, 1 stop, no parity, FIFOs enabled\nUART0_LCRH_R = 0x70;\n// Enable UART0\nUART0_CTL_R |= 0x01;
Annotation
  • Clock enables ensure the peripheral registers are functional.
  • Alternate function and digital enable switch pin modes from GPIO to UART.
  • IBRD and FBRD set the baud generator; they come from the baud calculation.
Terminal test
Hello, Embedded World!\r\n
Pro tip

After initialization, send a simple known string to confirm all steps worked. If you see nothing, re-check clock and pin settings before changing baud divisors.

Common mistake

Not waiting for clock stabilization or leaving PA0/PA1 as GPIO will result in no output.

screens.title: Baud rate and divisor calculation
screens.subtitle: How IBRD and FBRD are derived for a given system clock

narration.text: Baud rate defines how many bits per second are sent over the line. The UART on the TM4C family uses a baud-rate divisor with an integer part and a fractional part. The formula shown in the source material is BRD equals system clock divided by sixteen times the desired baud. The integer portion is the value written to UARTIBRD, and the fractional portion multiplied by sixty-four and rounded becomes UARTFBRD. For example, with a 16 megahertz system clock and a desired baud of 115200, BRD equals 16,000,000 divided by (16 times 115200) which evaluates to about 8.6805. The integer divisor becomes 8 and the fractional 0.6805 times 64 rounds to 44, producing IBRD=8 and FBRD=44. A common misconception is that you can ignore the fractional part; skipping it makes baud error larger and can produce unreadable output. Another practical point: when asked to compute divisors for 9600 baud with a 16 MHz clock, follow the same formula to produce IBRD=104 and FBRD=11 as shown in the assessment idea. Takeaway: accurate divisors reduce bit timing error and prevent garbled data at the terminal.

keyIdea.title: Baud divisor formula
keyIdea.text: BRD = SystemClock / (16 × Baud). IBRD = integer(BRD). FBRD = round((BRD - IBRD) × 64).

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Baud rate & divisors
Formula

Compute IBRD and FBRD

Use BRD = SystemClock / (16 × Baud). Extract integer part for IBRD. Multiply fractional part by 64 and round to get FBRD.

Example: 16 MHz, 115200 baud
BRD = 16000000 / (16 × 115200) = 8.6805\nIBRD = 8\nFBRD = round(0.6805 × 64) = 44
Common mistakes
  • Omitting the fractional divisor causes higher bit timing error.
  • Using the wrong system clock in the calculation yields incorrect divisors.
  • Not rounding the fractional product properly changes the effective baud slightly.
Assessment example

For 16 MHz and 9600 baud: BRD = 104.1667, IBRD = 104, FBRD = round(0.1667 × 64) = 11. Use these to program the divisors.

screens.title: Serial framing: 8N1 and alternatives
screens.subtitle: Data bits, parity, and stop bits influence compatibility

narration.text: Serial framing defines how each byte is packaged on the line. The configuration 8N1 — eight data bits, no parity, one stop bit — is the common default used in the example code. Eight data bits provide a full byte for ASCII printing. No parity simplifies configuration and is fine for debugging because occasional single-bit errors are less critical when messages are short and repeated. One stop bit gives a single-bit gap between frames. Alternatives include adding a parity bit to detect single-bit errors or increasing stop bits to provide extra spacing for slower receivers. A useful way to think about framing is to compare two cases: 8N1 and 7E1 (seven data bits, even parity, one stop bit). While 7E1 can help catch small errors, it changes how bytes map to characters and will show gibberish if the receiver uses 8N1. A common misconception is that parity corrects errors — parity only detects a single-bit mismatch and cannot correct it. For most debugging prints, 8N1 at an agreed baud is the simplest and most interoperable choice. Your takeaway: always confirm terminal settings match the UART line control to avoid garbled output.

keyIdea.title: Framing matters
keyIdea.text: Both ends must agree on data bits, parity, and stop bits. 8N1 is the typical default for debugging text output.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Serial framing
Comparison

8N1 vs 7E1

8N1
  • 8 data bits
  • No parity
  • 1 stop bit
  • Best for ASCII text debugging
7E1
  • 7 data bits
  • Even parity
  • 1 stop bit
  • Useful when parity is required for error detection
If the board sends 8N1 but the terminal listens with parity enabled, characters will appear wrong. Always match framing exactly.
Timing diagram (conceptual)
[ start ] [ d0 d1 d2 d3 d4 d5 d6 d7 ] [ stop ]
Misconception check

Parity detects some single-bit errors but does not correct them. It can reduce undetected errors but cannot guarantee clean characters if framing mismatches occur.

Key Takeaway

Choose 8N1 for straightforward debugging; only change framing when you intentionally require parity or different data widths.

screens.title: Sending characters and strings
screens.subtitle: Safe transmit using the flag register and a send-string routine

narration.text: Sending characters safely requires checking the UART flag register to ensure the transmit FIFO is not full. The example code uses a loop that waits while the TX FIFO full flag is set, and then writes the character to the data register. This pattern prevents overwriting the FIFO and losing characters. The send-string routine simply iterates through a null-terminated string and calls the send-char routine for each byte. A concrete example: sending the string "Hello, Embedded World!" writes each ASCII character in sequence, ending with carriage return and newline so the terminal moves to the next line. A common misconception is that one write will always succeed immediately; on busy systems the FIFO may be full and a write could be ignored or block, so the check is necessary. For interactive debugging you may also want a receive routine that polls the flag register for data available, so the device can respond to simple commands. Takeaway: implement small, well-tested send and send-string functions as the foundation for printf-style debugging. Sending characters and strings means wait for tx fifo not-full using uartfr before writing to uartdr; iterate for strings.. In practical terms, safe transmit using the flag register and a send-string routine. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transmit pattern
keyIdea.text: Wait for TX FIFO not-full using UARTFR before writing to UARTDR; iterate for strings.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Sending characters
Send routine
void UART0_SendChar(char c) {\n // Wait until transmit FIFO is not full\n while ((UART0_FR_R & UART_FR_TXFF) != 0) {}\n UART0_DR_R = c;\n}\n\nvoid UART0_SendString(char *str) {\n while (*str) {\n UART0_SendChar(*str);\n str++;\n }\n}
This code waits for the TX full flag to clear, then writes the byte. The string routine walks a null-terminated array and sends each character in turn.
Terminal example
Hello, Embedded World!\r\n
Misconception check

Assuming writes always succeed immediately can hide transient issues. Use the flag check to prevent overwrites and lost characters.

Key Takeaway

Simple send routines are reliable and portable; build on them to implement higher-level logging or printf helpers.

screens.title: UART registers you must know
screens.subtitle: What UARTIBRD, UARTFBRD, UARTLCRH, UARTCTL, UARTDR, and UARTFR do

narration.text: Understanding the UART registers is essential to control behavior and diagnose problems. UARTIBRD and UARTFBRD hold the integer and fractional baud divisors that drive the baud generator. UARTLCRH defines line control: data bits, parity, stop bits, and FIFO enable. UARTCTL is the control register that enables or disables the UART transmitter and receiver. UARTDR is the data register: write to it to send a byte and read from it to receive a byte. UARTFR is the flag register that tells you status like whether the transmit FIFO is full or whether data is available to read. A typical diagnostic flow is to read UARTFR, see if TXFF is set, and wait; then write UARTDR. If you never see output, check that UARTCTL indicates the UART is enabled and that the clock gating registers were previously set. The common misconception is thinking a single register controls everything — in reality, configuration and data flow are handled across several registers. Concrete example: after setting UARTIBRD and UARTFBRD for 115200, set UARTLCRH to 0x70 to choose 8 data bits and enable FIFOs, then set UARTCTL to turn on the peripheral. Final takeaway: map each visible problem to the register most likely responsible — baud problems point to IBRD/FBRD, framing problems to LCRH, and silence to CTL or clock gating.

keyIdea.title: Register responsibilities
keyIdea.text: IBRD/FBRD control baud, LCRH controls framing, CTL enables the peripheral, DR moves data, FR reports status.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › UART Registers
Architecture

Key registers

  • UARTIBRD / UARTFBRD: integer and fractional divisors for baud generation.
  • UARTLCRH: line control, data bits, parity, stop bits, and FIFO enable.
  • UARTCTL: control register to enable TX and RX.
  • UARTDR: data register for sending and receiving bytes.
  • UARTFR: flag register for status bits like transmit FIFO full.
Concrete example

After calculating divisors for 115200, write IBRD=8 and FBRD=44. Set LCRH to 0x70 to request 8N1 with FIFOs. Then set CTL to enable the UART. If you still see nothing, check SYSCTL clock gating for UART0 and GPIO Port A.

Troubleshooting tip

If output is garbled, first check divisors and system clock. If there is no output at all, confirm the UARTCTL enable bit and the GPIO alternate function for PA0/PA1.

Key Takeaway

Divide responsibilities across registers: divisors for baud, LCRH for framing, CTL for enabling, DR/FR for data and status.

screens.title: Building printf-style debugging
screens.subtitle: From send-char to formatted text — a practical approach

narration.text: Printf-style debugging in a constrained embedded environment is often implemented by composing simpler functions. Start with a reliable UART0_SendChar that waits for the transmit FIFO to be available before writing a byte. Then implement UART0_SendString which iterates through a C string and calls the send-char routine. For numeric values, write small helper functions that convert integers to ASCII digits and send them. For example, to print a counter you can convert the integer to its decimal representation and call the send-string routine for the digits followed by carriage return and newline. This approach avoids heavyweight library support and gives you deterministic control over what is sent. A common misconception is that printf from a desktop C library is free to use; in many embedded contexts, standard printf pulls in large libraries and may not be available. Instead, a minimal formatted printer that supports only the conversions you need — numbers and simple strings — is more practical. A practical test: print a counter from 0 to 100 with a small delay and verify the terminal output. Takeaway: build small, testable helpers to make a custom printf that is compact and dependable.

keyIdea.title: Composition approach
keyIdea.text: Start with send-char, compose send-string, add integer-to-ascii helper, and form small printf-like helpers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Printf-style debugging
Design pattern

Small helpers compose into printf

// send-char and send-string as before\n// integer to ascii (very small)\nvoid UART0_SendUnsigned(uint32_t value) {\n char buf[11];\n int i = 0;\n if (value==0) { UART0_SendChar('0'); return; }\n while (value) { buf[i++]= '0' + (value % 10); value/=10; }\n while (i--) UART0_SendChar(buf[i]);\n}
This minimal integer formatter prints unsigned decimals and can be combined with send-string to produce messages like "count=42" followed by newline for readability in the terminal.
Practical example
count=0\r\ncount=1\r\n...\r\ncount=100\r\n
Misconception check

Do not assume desktop printf is suitable for small microcontrollers. Implement only the features you need to keep code size and complexity low.

Key Takeaway

A few small, tested helpers give you robust debugging prints without large library overhead.

screens.title: Hands-on: count 0 to 100 and monitor switches
screens.subtitle: A test program to validate UART and observe runtime state

narration.text: A practical activity consolidates configuration and send routines: initialize UART0, then print numbers from 0 to 100, each on its own line. This verifies baud, framing, and pin setup. Start by calling UART0_Init from main. Next, in a loop convert the loop index to ASCII and send it followed by carriage return and newline. Observe the output in a PC terminal at 115200 with 8N1. After you confirm the counting, extend the program to print a switch state or a counter variable alongside the number. For example, read a switch input and print its value next to the counter: this helps you correlate input changes with program events. A common pitfall is forgetting to include small delays or yields if the terminal cannot keep up, but for counting to 100 at moderate speed this is usually unnecessary. This activity teaches you to separate configuration problems from logic problems: if no numbers appear, focus on initialization; if numbers appear but switch states are wrong, debug input reading. Final question: when the terminal shows occasional missing lines, what would you inspect first — the TX FIFO fullness or terminal baud framing?

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Print a counted sequence to confirm UART0 is configured and extend it to show switch state for a simple runtime check.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Hands-on Activity
Task

Count 0 to 100 over UART

int main(void) {\n UART0_Init();\n for (int i=0;i<=100;i++) {\n UART0_SendUnsigned(i);\n UART0_SendString("\r\n");\n // optional: read switch and print its state\n }\n while(1) {}\n}
Open a terminal at 115200, set 8N1, and verify you see each number on its own line. Extend the loop to print a switch read value to practice combining inputs and prints.
Verification steps
  1. Upload firmware and ensure the board is powered via USB debugger.
  2. Open the correct virtual COM port in your terminal program.
  3. Set terminal settings to 115200, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit.
  4. Observe the sequence 0 to 100; if missing, re-check initialization and TX FIFO handling.
Troubleshooting tip

If output is present but numbers repeat or skip, check whether your loop runs faster than the UART can transmit and ensure you wait for the transmit FIFO as shown in the example code.

screens.title: Common errors and how to diagnose them
screens.subtitle: A checklist to map observable symptoms to likely causes

narration.text: When serial output is missing or incorrect, a short diagnostic checklist maps symptoms to likely root causes. Symptom one: no output at all. Likely causes include forgetting to enable the UART or GPIO clocks, failing to set the alternate function on PA0/PA1, or not enabling the UART via the control register. Symptom two: garbled or unreadable characters. Look first at baud divisor calculations — incorrect IBRD/FBRD are the usual culprit — and then confirm terminal framing settings like 8N1. Symptom three: sporadic or missing characters. This often indicates that the transmit FIFO was overrun because code wrote without checking the TX full flag, or the device is producing output faster than the terminal can process. Symptom four: correct text but wrong values for variables. In that case the issue is in measurement code, not the UART, so add more prints near sensor reads to localize the bug. A frequent misconception is assuming the USB cable or terminal program is always correct; while possible, verify peripheral and pin configuration first. Takeaway: use symptoms to choose which register or code location to inspect next, and use small incremental tests to confirm fixes.

keyIdea.title: Diagnostics checklist

screens.title: Calculate divisors for a different baud rate
screens.subtitle: Practice: compute IBRD and FBRD for 9600 baud at 16 MHz

narration.text: The assessment idea in the chapter asks you to compute the integer and fractional baud divisors for a 16 megahertz system clock and a desired baud of 9600. Follow the same formula: BRD equals system clock divided by sixteen times the baud. Plugging in numbers gives BRD equals 16,000,000 divided by 153,600 which is about 104.1667. The integer divisor IBRD is therefore 104. The fractional portion is 0.1667; multiply by 64 and round to obtain FBRD equals 11. That pair, IBRD=104 and FBRD=11, configures the baud generator for 9600 with minimal timing error. A practical check is to program these values, open a terminal at 9600 with 8N1, and send a known string. If characters appear slow but readable, your divisors are likely correct. If they are slightly off, double-check the system clock used in the calculation — an incorrect clock assumption is the most common source of an incorrect divisor. Takeaway: the divisor formula is the same for all speeds — change only the baud value and recompute the integer and fractional parts. Calculate divisors for a different baud rate means for 16 mhz and 9600 baud: brd ≈ 104.1667 → ibrd = 104, fbrd = 11. verify in a terminal at 9600, 8n1.. Clocks & Pins

Always enable UART0 and GPIO clocks and set PA0/PA1 to alternate function before initializing the UART.

Divisors & Framing
